action: Search your GitHub organisations for wfx-docs branches and pull requests titled 'docs: dependency audit notes', and look for gaps in workflow run numbers. Where the payload ran, rotate every secret and cloud role those workflows could reach.
exec: Hijacked developer accounts are being used to plant key-stealing code in software projects, a risk for any team building on GitHub.
plain: Attackers used 4,837 taken-over GitHub accounts to probe more than 61,000 code projects and ran password-stealing code in the build systems of at least 1,835 of them.

key_findings: From about 12:45 UTC on November 10, 4,837 compromised GitHub accounts opened probe pull requests in 61,764 repositories to test for write access.
At least 1,835 repositories ran the payload and had credentials taken; the true figure may be higher because run logs were deleted.
The stealer arrives through an altered workflow, an npm postinstall hook or a throwaway workflow, and is reverted within about a minute.
It takes Actions secrets, cloud and registry credentials and AI provider keys, then pivots into AWS, GCP, Azure, Vault and Kubernetes.
New tricks include forged success status checks, rewritten AWS role trust policies and Azure federated credentials named wfx-ci for persistence.
recommendations: Search for wfx-docs branches and pull requests titled 'docs: dependency audit notes'.
Check for gaps in workflow run numbers, which may be the only trace of a run.
If the payload ran, rotate every secret and cloud role available to that repository's workflows.
Review AWS role trust policies and remove Azure federated credentials named wfx-ci.
Treat machines that installed the affected Packagist or Go module versions as compromised.

recommendations: Control who can access patient records, and grant, review and remove access appropriately.
Monitor and audit systems to detect suspicious access.

Investigate suspected cases promptly, keep affected people informed and act where wrongdoing is found.
If no review was done in the past six months, complete one within three months.

action: Follow Unit 42's guidance: tighten identity hygiene (strong unique passwords, no shared or default credentials), cut internet-facing attack surface, patch dated public flaws, and add the two published IP indicators to monitoring.
exec: AI-run intrusions got in through weak passwords, open cloud storage and login bypasses, not new exploits; basic identity and patch upkeep is the defence.
plain: Unit 42 says a likely China-linked group used an AI hacking tool to run 25 mostly automated break-in attempts on at least 19 chip, defence and civil-society bodies, got into 10 and accessed more than one million union member records.

key_findings: Targets were 7 semiconductor and advanced-manufacturing firms, 3 defence or defence-policy bodies and 4 human-rights or civil-society groups, including a Canadian rights body and a US teachers' union.
The cluster ran 25 operations against at least 19 organisations and reached confirmed unauthorised access or data retrieval at 10 of them.
It used a customised fork of the open-source Cairn framework driven by Zhipu GLM 5.2 and DeepSeek V4 models, plus a custom skill pack not in upstream Cairn.
Entry came from password spraying, brute-forced credentials, unauthenticated cloud-storage writes, login bypasses and open registration endpoints rather than new exploits.

At a US teachers' union the framework logged access to more than one million member records, roughly 31,000 CRM contacts and staff password hashes; Unit 42 assesses China-nexus collection with moderate confidence.
recommendations: Tighten identity hygiene: remove weak, default and shared passwords on internet-facing applications.
Reduce the exposed attack surface, including open registration endpoints and unauthenticated cloud storage.
Patch software affected by older public CVEs.
Monitor for the two IP addresses Unit 42 published for the Cairn hosting and staging servers.

summary: Unit 42 tracked a cluster, CL-STA-1238, running a customised fork of the open-source Cairn AI penetration-testing framework on Chinese AI models. It ran 25 operations against at least 19 organisations in the semiconductor supply chain, defence and civil society, with confirmed access or data retrieval at 10. At a US teachers' union it logged access to more than one million member records. Unit 42 assesses China-nexus intelligence collection with moderate confidence.
title: Unit 42: autonomous 'Cairn' operations hit semiconductor, defense and civil-society targets

validation.note: Primary source: the Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 report (12 Nov), re-read on 22 Nov with no update note; AgentBeam timeline tracker removed from sources.

review.note: Compared 25 ops/19 orgs/10 accessed, over 1M records, moderate-confidence China-nexus, models, IPs, date 12 Nov against the Unit 42 report.

evidence.quote: conduct 25 operations against at least 19 organizations
These attacks achieved unauthorized access or data retrieval at 10 of the targeted organizations.
The framework logged access to more than one million member records, roughly 31,000 CRM contacts and staff password hashes.
Unit 42 assesses with moderate confidence that CL-STA-1238 represents a China-nexus intelligence collection campaign.

action: Barracuda Managed XDR Cloud or Monitored Endpoint customers who were contacted: revoke and recreate API integration credentials. Everyone: retire long-lived keys held by third parties, use short-lived scoped credentials, and rehearse rotating secrets at scale.
exec: A forgotten key held by a supplier let an automated attacker into a security vendor; some XDR customers were asked to reissue credentials.
plain: Barracuda says an old access key it had left with an outside AI supplier was used to get into about 10 of its cloud accounts for under two days in early November, using an automated AI attack tool.

key_findings: The attacker used a cloud access key Barracuda had issued to a third-party AI vendor for a past project and never retired; the vendor's development environment was compromised in October.
Activity ran from November 1 04:33 UTC to November 2 23:31 UTC and touched about 10 cloud accounts; it was noticed on November 4 after it had stopped.
The attacker hunted secrets, infrastructure state files and Kubernetes credentials, deployed a container mounting the host filesystem, and was blocked from creating a new admin identity.
One reachable system held credentials Barracuda XDR uses to collect customer data; no direct evidence of access was found but logging could not rule it out.
Barracuda attributes the method, not the actor, to the open-source ARTEX AI penetration-testing framework.
recommendations: Remove standing credentials, especially long-lived keys held by third parties; use short-lived, narrowly scoped ones.
Limit blast radius so no single credential opens the next system.
Assume compromise and be able to rotate secrets at scale and rebuild from known-good states.
Customers contacted by Barracuda should revoke and recreate Managed XDR API integration credentials.

summary: Barracuda's CISO says an attacker used a cloud access key the company had given a third-party AI vendor for a past project and never retired. From November 1 to 2 the attacker touched about 10 cloud accounts, harvested secrets and planted a container in a Kubernetes cluster. Activity matched the ARTEX framework. Barracuda rotated all reachable credentials and asked some Managed XDR customers to recreate integration credentials.
title: Barracuda links breach of its cloud accounts to ARTEX AI attack framework

action: Mobile operators: deploy GTP-C and GTP-U security aligned with SS7 and Diameter firewalls, treat the IPX interface as untrusted, and monitor internal signalling, not only the edge. High-risk users: avoid SMS login codes.
exec: Phone networks themselves were compromised, so calls and SMS codes can be intercepted without touching the handset.
plain: Telecom security firm Enea says one hacking group took over parts of Asian phone networks to intercept calls and texts, mostly of people in Taiwan, while a second group hid spying tools inside operators' data links.

key_findings: SilentAir ran attacks from compromised SS7 and Diameter nodes inside operators in at least six Asian countries, reaching a dozen more countries with Taiwan the main target.
It redirects subscribers' location registration to intercept calls and SMS, with one-time codes seen arriving right after interception; some targets were political and government VIPs.
Enea assesses with high confidence that SilentAir is a state-level actor and, at low confidence, China-aligned; it works a UTC+8 pattern and avoids Chinese networks.
LIMINAL PANDA uses GTPDoor implants, including a new variant hiding commands in GTP-U traffic, for covert control and exfiltration tunnels between infected operators.
Enea saw several hundred covert command attempts since Q1 2026 and at least 5 to 10 infected operators, possibly several dozen worldwide.
recommendations: Deploy GTP-C and GTP-U security and align it with SS7 and Diameter firewalls for cross-protocol visibility.
Treat the IPX interface as untrusted and inspect all traffic more deeply.
Monitor internal signalling protocols and tools, not just the network edge.
Integrate signalling security with IT security and reconsider outsourcing of core networks.

summary: Enea describes two actors inside mobile networks. SilentAir, assessed as state-level, used compromised SS7 and Diameter nodes in at least six Asian countries to redirect and intercept calls and texts, mainly of Taiwanese subscribers, including one-time codes. LIMINAL PANDA used GTPDoor implants for covert command traffic and data theft between operators; Enea saw at least 5 to 10 infected operators. A link between the two is unconfirmed.
title: SilentAir and LIMINAL PANDA exploit mobile networks to spy on subscribers

validation.note: Reviewed against the original Enea report.

action: Schools and universities: check whether your accounts appear in stolen-credential data, reset those passwords through a trusted process, revoke sessions, review mailbox rules and turn on phishing-resistant sign-in. Monitor outbound mail for bulk sending.
exec: Stolen staff or student logins can be reused to send threats under an institution's name, causing disruption and reputational harm.
plain: Schools across Europe received threatening emails on November 11. Researchers found that two university email addresses reported as senders, in Egypt and Taiwan, had already appeared in stolen-password data.

key_findings: Hudson Rock found two university addresses reported as senders of the threats, one Egyptian and one Taiwanese, in previously stolen credential data.
The Egyptian address sits in a Vidar infostealer record dated October 1, 2021, with 112 saved credentials, 20 of them using that address.
The Taiwanese address appears in the AlienTXTBASE collection, more than a year old; the university later saw abnormal bulk sending and suspended the account.
About 6,000 Italian schools received the messages, more than 300 in Northern Ireland, with threats also reported in Scotland and Ireland.
Hudson Rock says this shows earlier exposure, not proof the credentials were used, and attributes the threats to no person, group or state.
recommendations: Contain any affected account and reset its credentials through a trusted process.
Revoke sessions and refresh tokens and review app passwords, sign-in methods, app consents and mailbox rules.
Investigate and clean the infected device.
Move to phishing-resistant sign-in and monitor outbound mail for bulk sending.
Use leaked-credential detection and risk-based access policies.

summary: Threat emails reached about 6,000 Italian schools (per ANSA, citing the Education Ministry) and more than 300 in Northern Ireland (PSNI) on November 11; threats were also reported in Scotland and Ireland. Hudson Rock found two university addresses reported as senders, one Egyptian and one Taiwanese, in infostealer data that predates the threats by a year or more. It stresses this shows earlier credential exposure, not proof of use, and names no culprit.
title: School bomb-threat emails across Europe traced to accounts found in infostealer data

action: After any web server compromise, remove the GSocket client, its persistence and staged files, then confirm relay connections have stopped. Apply deny-by-default outbound rules and audit cron entries, systemd units and shell startup files.
attack: T1059.004 Command and Scripting Interpreter: Unix Shell
exec: Patching a hacked web server is not enough; a relay tool left behind keeps attackers in, and it has no fixed address to block.
plain: Microsoft warns that hackers who break into Linux web servers are leaving behind a free relay tool that keeps them connected even after the original hole is fixed.

key_findings: Internet-facing Linux web servers are the target; Among web-application and hosting incidents, PHP applications and cPanel hosting account for 63.9% and Apache for 24.3%.
Education and research is the most affected sector at 30.7% of organisations, which Microsoft attributes to exposure rather than deliberate targeting.
After web application code execution, a curl download-and-run script installs GSocket, which connects outbound to a shared public relay.
Access persists after the original flaw is patched, and there is no attacker-owned address or domain to block.
Devices with GSocket detections rose 356.2% from March to August 2026; in few observed incidents attackers also tried the Dirty Frag flaw CVE-2026-43284 to gain root.
recommendations: Remediate the host, not just the vulnerability: remove the GSocket client, persistence and staged files and confirm relay connections stop.
Apply deny-by-default egress rules and monitor connections to relay infrastructure.
Mount temporary and memory-backed directories as non-executable and alert on execution from hidden or world-writable paths.
Audit cron entries, systemd units and shell startup files.
Hunt for gs-netcat or gsocket processes and staging files under /dev/shm.

summary: Microsoft says multiple unrelated attackers are installing the open-source GSocket tool on Linux web servers after exploiting web applications. Both the server and the attacker connect outbound to a shared public relay, so there is no attacker address to block and access survives patching of the original flaw. Devices with GSocket detections rose 356.2% between March and August 2026, with PHP and cPanel hosting most affected.
title: Microsoft: attackers use open-source GSocket to keep hidden access to hacked Linux servers

validation.note: Reviewed against the original Microsoft Threat Intelligence report.

review.note: Checked against Microsoft post: 63.9%/24.3% are shares within web-app/hosting incidents and 356.2% is devices with detections, Dirty Frag only in few incidents; wording fixed

The advisory lists 46 CVEs, 37 of them in FortiManager and FortiAnalyzer.
The most severe flaws could allow arbitrary code execution, with impact depending on the privileges of the affected account.
No exploitation in the wild had been reported at publication.
Risk is rated High for government and business entities of every size and Low for home users.
recommendations: Apply Fortinet's updates to vulnerable systems immediately after appropriate testing.
Keep network infrastructure on current, supported software and remediate detected vulnerabilities at least monthly.
Apply least privilege and disable or secure default accounts.
Use dedicated, segmented, non-internet-connected systems for administrative work.

action: Identify Linux systems running OpenSSH before 10.6p2 on musl libc without PAM that accept password logins, and update to 10.6p2. Until then, disable password authentication or turn SSH off on those systems.
exec: The flaw applies only to a narrow combination of settings, but where all four conditions hold the result may be root access.
plain: New Zealand's cyber agency warned of a flaw in OpenSSH, the standard tool for logging in to Linux machines remotely, that could let an attacker in as the top-level user on certain lightweight Linux systems.

key_findings: CVE-2026-123158, also called SSHole, is an authentication bypass in OpenSSH on Linux that may allow root access.
All four conditions must hold: version earlier than 10.6p2, musl libc, no Pluggable Authentication Modules, and password logins accepted.
OpenSSH 10.6p2 fixes the flaw.
The alert gives no CVSS score and does not say whether the flaw is being exploited.
recommendations: Update to OpenSSH 10.6p2.
As mitigation, disable password authentication or disable SSH.
Identify potentially affected systems in your environment.
Apply vendor patches or mitigations as they become available and follow the OpenSSH release notes.

summary: New Zealand's NCSC issued an alert on November 11 about CVE-2026-123158, nicknamed SSHole, an authentication bypass in OpenSSH on Linux that may give an attacker root access. A system is exposed only if it runs a version before 10.6p2, uses musl libc, does not use PAM and accepts password logins. The alert does not say whether the flaw is being exploited.
title: NCSC New Zealand alerts on OpenSSH 'SSHole' authentication bypass CVE-2026-123158

action: UK critical infrastructure, government and larger organisations: use the NCSC's Find a Provider page to choose an assured CyAS supplier, and consider adversary simulation alongside the Cyber Assessment Framework and Cyber Resilience Audit.
exec: UK critical-sector bodies get an assured route to adversary-simulation testing; regulators may use it as common evidence.
plain: Britain's cyber agency started a scheme that vets companies offering realistic mock attacks, so important organisations can choose a trusted firm to test their defences.

key_findings: The NCSC launched the Cyber Adversary Simulation (CyAS) scheme, which assures suppliers of adversary simulation services against an NCSC-defined standard.
It is aimed at the UK's most critical organisations and their Cyber Oversight Bodies, with larger organisations, critical national infrastructure and government highlighted.
Providers do reconnaissance, build customer-specific attack plans and pursue agreed objectives without being limited to purchased threat intelligence or documented techniques.
CyAS complements the Cyber Assessment Framework and the Cyber Resilience Audit scheme and was developed with regulators and lead government departments.
The scheme launches as a minimum viable product so the NCSC can test demand and refine the method; the release names no providers.
recommendations: Use the scheme's Find a Provider page to identify assured adversary simulation providers.
Consider CyAS alongside the Cyber Assessment Framework and Cyber Resilience Audit to build a fuller picture of security and resilience.

summary: The UK's NCSC launched the Cyber Adversary Simulation (CyAS) scheme on November 11. It assesses commercial suppliers against an NCSC standard so that critical organisations, government and their oversight bodies can pick trusted providers to run realistic simulated attacks. It sits alongside the Cyber Assessment Framework and Cyber Resilience Audit scheme and starts as a minimum viable product while demand and method are tested.
title: NCSC (UK) launches Cyber Adversary Simulation scheme to assure attack-simulation providers

action: Review browser extensions installed in developer mode, especially utilities asking for broad permissions. Audit webmail and case-management pages for script tags loading from unfamiliar domains, and investigate OneDrive activity to tenants outside your organisation.
exec: Browser-based spying leaves few traces on disk, so endpoint tools can miss it; webmail portals and browser extensions need checking.
plain: Researchers found spies running hidden code inside the web browsers of government workers in the Middle East and Southeast Asia, stealing logins and reading email without leaving files on the computer.

key_findings: Targets were defence, interior and foreign ministries, a telecom provider and government email in the Middle East, plus police, justice, military and foreign affairs bodies in Southeast Asia.
Falcon C2 runs JavaScript in the victim's browser over encrypted WebSockets to steal passwords, cookies and email and to proxy through logged-in sessions.
Entry methods were script tags injected into a ministry's Roundcube webmail (39 instances affected), a fake Flash update and a sideloaded 'PDF Viewer' extension requesting 40 permissions.
A Rust implant named Antino uses Microsoft OneDrive as its command channel.
Unit 42 assesses with high confidence that Falcon and the earlier PeckBirdy framework are variants of one core; it names no actor.
recommendations: Review extensions installed in developer mode that pose as utilities and request permissions such as all URLs, debugger or native messaging.
Audit webmail, ticketing and case-management pages for script tags loading from unfamiliar external domains.
Look for web-analytics style cookies or storage keys on internal apps where analytics has no reason to appear.
Investigate OAuth activity to OneDrive tenants outside your organisation, especially repeated small JSON writes.

summary: Unit 42 reports that a framework called Falcon C2 ran malicious JavaScript inside the browsers of government staff in one Middle Eastern and four Southeast Asian countries between March and May 2026. It steals passwords, cookies and email, and lets attackers browse as the victim. Delivery included injected scripts on a foreign ministry's Roundcube webmail and a fake PDF viewer extension. No actor is named.
title: Unit 42: Falcon C2 turns victims' browsers into spying tools at Middle East and Asian ministries

action: Government, telecom and critical infrastructure security teams: load Check Point's published indicators, hunt for the listed registry and firewall artifacts, and warn staff that a browser certificate error offering a fix installer is a lure.
actor: CopperDragon (tool developer for China-nexus groups, moderate confidence)
exec: Shared tooling across China-linked espionage groups means a detection for one campaign may help against the others.
plain: Check Point found that three separate spying campaigns in Europe, Asia and Latin America used related malicious software from one developer, which appears to supply several China-linked hacking groups.

key_findings: Check Point tracks the builder of the Sparrow framework as CopperDragon, a possible tool supplier to China-nexus groups including FamousSparrow, Earth Estries and Tropic Trooper; confidence is moderate.
SilentDelivery hit government, shipping and IT targets in Europe and Asia from early 2026 using watering-hole sites with a fake Chrome certificate error and a bogus fix installer.
OceanGate targeted government and critical infrastructure in Asia through an internet-facing Linux server, then RDP password attempts against Windows administrators.
DarkWire has targeted telecom providers and foreign affairs and justice ministries in Latin America since mid-2025; its link to the group is weaker.
New tools include SquadC, AnnobinDoor, SparrowShell with an embedded Linux kernel rootkit, CopperDNS, and a passive backdoor hiding on a legitimate port.
recommendations: Hunt for the host artifacts Check Point lists, including a WindowsUpdateAssist Run key and firewall rules named RasiUwpApp and ss1.
Check for an unexpected LocalAccountTokenFilterPolicy change and an account named admin$.
Load the published hashes, domains, addresses and certificate details into detection.

For the Outlook flaw the Preview Pane is not an attack vector and MSRC lists no mitigation or workaround.
recommendations: Install the November 10 security update for every affected Outlook version; Microsoft lists no workaround.
Tell users not to open unexpected message files sent as attachments, since opening is the trigger.
Apply the updates for the Critical 9.8 remote code execution flaws in Windows LDAP, Windows Search and Xbox Live Networking Service.

Apply least privilege and disable or secure default accounts.
Segment the network and administer devices from dedicated resources without internet access.

plain: SAP's monthly security release includes four flaws given the highest possible severity score. SAP's own records confirm an attacker needs no login to use them. Fixes are available.

key_findings: SAP's own CVE records rate four flaws CVSS 10.0, each exploitable over the network without authentication or user interaction.
CVE-2026-76964 (NetWeaver AS ABAP Internet Communication Manager) and CVE-2026-89126 (Web Dispatcher) are memory corruption from crafted network traffic that could give code execution.
CVE-2026-89103: SAP Gateway turns on a high-privilege default access control list that can treat an outside attacker as an internal application server.
CVE-2026-120017: under certain configurations the SAML2 service provider does not properly verify assertions, letting an attacker impersonate any user including privileged ones.
Affected kernels span 7.53 to 9.20 for ICM and Web Dispatcher, 7.22 to 9.21 for Gateway, and SAP_BASIS 702 to 922 for SAML2.
report.publisher: SAP (CVE records published by SAP as CVE numbering authority)
recommendations: Apply SAP Note 3778530 (NetWeaver AS ABAP ICM) and SAP Note 3778556 (Web Dispatcher).
Apply SAP Note 3798345 (SAP Gateway).
Apply SAP Note 3849308 (SAML2 service provider in AS ABAP and ABAP Platform).

summary: SAP's November 10 CVE records confirm four flaws rated CVSS 10.0: memory corruption in the NetWeaver AS ABAP Internet Communication Manager and in Web Dispatcher, a SAP Gateway default access list that can treat outsiders as internal servers, and a SAML2 assertion check failure allowing impersonation of any user. Each is fixed by its own SAP Note. The 35-note total comes from secondary coverage.
title: SAP Patch Day: 35 notes, four rated CVSS 10.0

action: Teams running their own Exchange servers, especially in government: check servers against ESET's published indicators in its malware-ioc GitHub repository and inspect transport agents and unexpected .NET assemblies; network detection alone is unreliable here.
attack: T1114.002 Email Collection: Remote Email Collection
exec: The malware never calls out; it lives inside the Exchange server and blends with normal mail traffic, so network monitoring alone will not catch it.
plain: ESET found new spying tools from the Russia-aligned Turla group on government email servers in Kazakhstan and Romania. The tools hide inside the mail server and copy messages exchanged with NATO and EU bodies.

key_findings: ESET attributes the Cereal toolset to Turla (Snake) with high confidence, citing concurrent use of a known Turla component and similarity to older Turla malware.
Victims are two national government organisations: Kazakhstan (found November 28, 2025) and Romania (compromised December 23, 2025).
CerealNeuron is a passive backdoor that listens for web requests on Exchange-like paths, so there is no outbound command traffic to spot.
CerealBox is injected into the Exchange transport process and wraps transport agent handlers to stage mail; in Romania it collected messages involving NATO and EU addresses.
The post does not say how the attackers first got in; fuller analysis is in a separate ESET white paper.
recommendations: Check Exchange servers against the indicators ESET publishes in its malware-ioc GitHub repository.
Do not rely on network detection: the traffic uses OWA, Autodiscover and ActiveSync paths and blends with legitimate Exchange traffic.

summary: ESET Research attributes, with high confidence, a previously unknown toolset called Cereal to Russia-aligned Turla. It was found on Exchange servers of two national government bodies: in Kazakhstan on November 28, 2025 and in Romania, compromised December 23, 2025. A passive backdoor listens on Exchange-like web paths, and a collector injected into the mail transport process staged messages involving NATO and EU addresses. Initial access is not described.
title: Turla uses new Cereal toolset to steal email from government Exchange servers

action: No patch exists. Limit who can run untrusted software with application control, do not disable CLFS authentication, deploy Cyderes's detections for the Defender update interface and unexpected hid.dll files, and apply Microsoft's fix when released.
exec: A public, unpatched Windows flaw raises the damage an attacker can do after any initial foothold; no fix is available yet.
plain: A researcher published an unfixed Windows flaw, named SignDrop, that lets someone who already has basic access to a computer gain full control of it by misusing built-in protections. No fix exists yet.

key_findings: A researcher using the name MSNightmare (Nightmare-Eclipse cluster) published SignDrop on GitHub on November 10, 2026 without coordinated disclosure.

It raises a standard user to SYSTEM without memory corruption, abusing CLFS HMAC authentication and the Defender signature-update RPC interface to plant a file, then sideloading a DLL through consent.exe.
Cyderes reproduced all five stages and got a SYSTEM shell with no UAC prompt; the exploit deletes its planted DLL afterwards.
No CVE or patch exists; Microsoft had not commented as of November 11 and no in-the-wild use was identified as of November 10.
It is the cluster's sixteenth public zero-day in about thirty-one weeks; the researcher's claim that about 80% of installations are vulnerable is unsupported.
recommendations: Inventory the CLFS Authentication Mode registry value across hosts to define which systems to prioritise.
Do not disable CLFS authentication, because that reopens older memory-corruption attack classes.
Restrict untrusted local code execution with application and script control.
Deploy the detections Cyderes lists, such as Defender signature-update RPC calls from outside the Defender service tree and any hid.dll created in the ink directory.
Retain file-creation and image-load telemetry, since the exploit removes its artifact.

summary: A researcher using the name MSNightmare published SignDrop on November 10, an unpatched Windows flaw that lifts a standard user to SYSTEM by abusing CLFS log authentication and Microsoft Defender's signature-update interface. Cyderes reproduced it in a controlled environment and got a SYSTEM shell. There is no CVE or patch; as of November 11 Microsoft had not commented, and no use in real attacks had been confirmed.
title: SignDrop: researcher releases Windows zero-day giving SYSTEM privileges

action: Take SSH off the internet and require two-factor sign-in for remote access. Patch VMware vCenter and anything still exposed to Log4Shell. Software makers: isolate signing servers and review their logs for unexpected use.
exec: Attackers were positioned for a supply-chain attack on a developer's customers; the signing step was blocked, but only just.
plain: Kaspersky found that a hacking group spent months inside a Russian software company and tried to tamper with the server that digitally signs its software. Security software blocked that attempt.

key_findings: The victim is a Russia-based developer of industrial software used mainly in Eastern Europe; Kaspersky attributes the intrusion to BO Team (Black Owl) with high confidence.
Entry was through internet-exposed SSH on a Linux terminal server with a password-authenticated service account; Log4Shell in vCenter 7.0.3 then gave root on a hypervisor.
Attackers stayed for several months and reached domain controllers, GitLab, the Ansible server, backups, SIEM and the mail server, stealing its DKIM private key.
Attempts to inject code on the code-signing server were blocked by security software; no signed malware distribution, encryption or destruction is reported.
The stolen DKIM key let them send phishing that passed sender checks, and they mostly lived off the land rather than deploying malware.
recommendations: Remove internet exposure of SSH, disable root SSH login and require two-factor sign-in for VPN, RDP and domain controllers.
Patch vCenter, hypervisors and any software still affected by Log4j.
After an intrusion reset all account passwords, reset krbtgt twice and reissue keys and certificates.
Keep backups on a non-domain server with separate credentials and test restores.
Keep logs at least 30 days and remove plaintext credentials from scripts and directory comments.

summary: Kaspersky ICS CERT describes a months-long intrusion at a Russian industrial software developer, attributed with high confidence to BO Team. The attackers entered through internet-exposed SSH, used Log4Shell in VMware vCenter to gain root on a hypervisor, and reached domain controllers, GitLab and the mail server. Their attempts to inject code on the code-signing server were blocked, and no tampered software release is reported.
title: BO Team spends months inside a Russian software developer, targets its build-signing server

title: Victorian privacy regulator finds Education Department breached privacy law after school-system breach
date_note: OVIC's investigation report is dated October 2026 with no day given; iTnews reported its findings on 7 October 2026, the earliest dated page read. IDM reported the same findings on 20 November 2026. The breach was notified to OVIC on 7 January 2026.
summary: Victoria's privacy regulator OVIC found in its October 2026 report that the Department of Education contravened Information Privacy Principles 4.1 and 4.2. Through one school's compromised IT system, an attacker took every government school student's name, school, year level, school email and encrypted password, and those of hundreds of thousands of former students. OVIC made seven recommendations due by 31 December 2026; the department says it accepts them.
plain: Victoria's privacy regulator found the state education department kept former students' login data and did not protect student data well enough before a breach.
exec: Keeping credentials of past users and incomplete vulnerability remediation can breach privacy law.
action: OVIC recommended the department review its retention of past students' credentials and strengthen how critical vulnerability advisories reach schools; organisations holding similar records can run the same review.
impact: Former students affected: hundreds of thousands, per OVIC.
